---
title: "Decision Models with tidyllm"
description: "Code many texts or pictures with fixed yes/no, choice or score questions and get a probability for each answer, so you read the uncertain ones first."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE
)
options(width = 90)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(tidyllm)
library(tidyverse)
```

A chat model writes text, one word at a time. A *decision model* reads a text and a fixed list of questions and answers each question without writing anything. Think of a trained coder filling in a coding form: one tick per question, either yes or no, one category, or a point on a scale. A decision model does the same job.

For each question you get one answer and a probability for it, between 0 and 1. A text with three questions gives three rows. Because the model writes no sentences, it is fast and cheap. Jev charges 0.042 US dollars per million input tokens (the pieces of text a model reads) and nothing for output tokens. A short survey answer plus our three questions is about 500 tokens, so coding 10,000 answers costs about 20 cents.

A decision model cannot explain itself. It gives no reasons, summaries or free text, and you must list every possible answer in advance. For explanations, quotes or labels you cannot list, use `chat()`.

**tidyllm** gives these models one verb, `decide()`. You write the questions once and change only the provider (`jev()`, `openai()`, `gemini()` or `ollama()`) to switch models. `jev()` is the decision model of TypeSafe AI and reads its key from `TYPESAFE_API_KEY`. Here we code eight invented survey answers with three questions: whether the answer is about economic policy, which topic it addresses, and how dissatisfied the writer is. Calls that need an API key are shown but not run; the next chunk loads the saved result. The [Get Started](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm.html) page explains API keys.

## Write your questions as a schema

You write each question as one field of a schema, a named list of questions. The field description is the question text, and the field type fixes the kind of answer.

| Function | Question type | The answer is |
|---|---|---|
| `field_lgl()` | yes/no | `yes` or `no` |
| `field_fct(.levels = )` | choice | one of your levels |
| `field_fct(.levels = , .ordered = TRUE)` | score | one of your levels; the order of the levels is the scale |

Only these helpers define questions for `decide()`; `field_box()` adds a third kind, described in the section on finding things in images. The [Get Started](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm.html) page explains schemas in general.

```{r questions_full}
questions <- tidyllm_schema(
  about_economy   = field_lgl("Does the answer mainly concern economic policy such as wages, taxes, rents or pensions?"),
  topic           = field_fct("Which topic does the answer mainly address?",
    .levels = c("housing", "labour", "taxes", "pensions", "migration", "climate", "none"),
    .level_descriptions = c("Rents, house prices, housing supply", "Wages, jobs, working conditions",
      "Tax rates and who pays them", "Pensions and old-age provision",
      "Immigration and integration", "Climate and energy policy", "No policy topic named")),
  dissatisfaction = field_fct("How strongly does the writer express dissatisfaction with current policy?",
    .levels = c("none", "mild", "strong"), .ordered = TRUE,
    .level_descriptions = c("No complaint", "Some criticism, measured tone", "Anger or a demand for urgent change"))
)
```

Three things to note in this schema:

- The model must pick one level, so add a `"none"` level for texts that fit no category.
- `.ordered = TRUE` makes a score question. List its levels from lowest to highest.
- `.level_descriptions` gives one short phrase per level. Models answer better when they know what each option means.

Very short texts need a framing sentence in front of the text that says what the material is, such as "Survey question: What is your job? Answer: ...". The [classifier article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html) shows what happens without it.

## Ask one text

The eight invented survey answers are stored in `decide_answers.rds` beside this article.

```{r answers_load}
answers <- read_rds("decide_answers.rds")

answers
```

One call returns one row per question. Run the first answer through Jev.

```{r one_call, eval = FALSE}
one <- decide(answers$text[1], questions, jev())
```

```{r one_call_saved, echo = FALSE}
one <- read_rds("decide_one.rds")
one |> select(question, type, answer, probability)
```

Read the rows like this. `type` says what kind of question it was. The model says yes to the economy question with probability 0.96, names housing as the topic at 1.00, and reports strong dissatisfaction at 1.00.

## Many texts at once

Pass a character vector and `decide()` codes every text. The calls run in parallel (at the same time) and come back as one tibble. A leading `state` column holds the text (cut to 60 characters) and `state_id` numbers the texts in the order you gave them.

```{r code_all, eval = FALSE}
many <- decide(answers$text, questions, jev())
```

```{r code_all_saved, echo = FALSE}
many <- read_rds("decide_many.rds")
```

Coding all eight answers with `jev()` took under a second in our run. Coding with the fastest OpenAI chat model was roughly ten times slower. A text that fails gives `NA` in `answer` and a warning that counts the failures, so you can filter on `is.na(answer)`, take the distinct `state_id` values and rerun only those texts.

Join the results to your data by `state_id`. The `coded` table has one row per answer and question, with `id` linking it to the respondent.

```{r join_ids}
coded <- answers |>
  mutate(state_id = row_number()) |>
  left_join(many, by = "state_id")

coded |>
  select(id, question, answer, probability) |>
  slice_head(n = 6)
```

For a regression you want one row per respondent. `pivot_wider()` puts each question in its own column.

```{r wide_table}
wide <- coded |>
  select(id, question, answer) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = question, values_from = answer)

wide
```

Join `wide` to the respondent data by `id`. The probabilities stay in `coded`, which the next section uses.

## Read the uncertain rows first

Treat the probability as a ranking: low means look twice. Sorting by it shows where to read first. Here `r sum(coded$probability < 0.8)` of the 24 answers have a probability below 0.8. That cut-off is a round number, not a rule.

```{r low_prob}
coded |>
  filter(probability < 0.8) |>
  select(id, question, answer, probability) |>
  arrange(probability)
```

A probability is *calibrated* when it matches how often the answer is right: of the answers given at 0.95, about 95 per cent should be correct. Check this on your own data with a hand-labelled sample. In the [classifier article](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html), 96 to 100 per cent of the answers above 0.95 matched the human label, against 51 to 62 per cent of the answers below 0.8.

## Images, audio and PDFs

`decide()` also reads photos, recordings and PDFs, with the same questions and the same result tibble. `provider_capabilities()` shows what each provider reads.

```{r media_capabilities}
provider_capabilities(.what = "decide_media") |>
  filter(supported) |>
  group_by(provider) |>
  summarise(reads = paste(media, collapse = ", "))
```

A provider that cannot read a file type stops with a message before anything is sent. Wrap a file in `img()` to give `decide()` a picture. The question says "the picture", because the picture is all the model sees.

```{r image_one, eval = FALSE}
cat_question <- tidyllm_schema(
  cat = field_lgl("Is the animal in the picture a cat?")
)

decide(img("photos/cat.jpg"), cat_question, openai(.detail = "low"))
```

`.detail = "low"` makes OpenAI read the picture at lower resolution, which is cheaper. Gemini has the same switch under the name `.resolution`.

To code many pictures, pass a list with one image per element; `map(files, img)` wraps each file in `img()`. Each element is its own item.

```{r image_many, eval = FALSE}
files <- list.files("photos", pattern = "jpg$", full.names = TRUE)

decide(map(files, img), cat_question, gemini(.resolution = "low"))
```

To ask about several files together, put them into one item: a named list inside the outer `list()`. The names label the parts, so the questions can say "photo_a" and "photo_b".

```{r image_two, eval = FALSE}
pets <- tidyllm_schema(
  a_dog = field_lgl("Is the animal in photo_a a dog?"),
  b_dog = field_lgl("Is the animal in photo_b a dog?")
)

decide(list(list(photo_a = img("photos/cat.jpg"), photo_b = img("photos/dog.jpg"))), pets, jev())
```

## Finding things in images (experimental)

Sometimes the question is "where is it", not "is there a cat". `field_box()` asks for one box around the thing. This is experimental: only `jev()` answers it, and the format may change in a later release. A box question always returns a box, even when the thing is not in the picture, so pair it with a yes/no question and read the box only where the answer is yes. Name the picture in a backticked key and in the question text.

```{r box_call, eval = FALSE}
where_cat <- tidyllm_schema(
  has_cat = field_lgl("Is there a cat in `photo`?"),
  cat = field_box("The cat in `photo`")
)

decide(list(list(photo = img("photos/cat.jpg"))), where_cat, jev())
```

```{r box_load, include = FALSE}
box_run <- readRDS("decide_box_result.rds")
```

```{r box_show}
box_run$result |>
  select(question, type, answer, probability, top, bottom, left, right)
```

The box row has type `box` and no answer. `top`, `bottom`, `left` and `right` are fractions of the picture, measured from the top-left corner. Here the cat starts at the left edge (`left` is 0) and reaches 79 per cent of the way to the right. The first row is the yes/no question, so its box columns are empty.

To draw or crop, you need pixels. `box_to_pixels()` multiplies the fractions by the image size.

```{r box_pixels}
box_to_pixels(box_run$result, .width = box_run$width, .height = box_run$height) |>
  select(question, x_min, x_max, y_min, y_max)
```

We have not measured how accurate boxes are. Look at a sample by eye before you rely on them.

## What to take away

- **Use `decide()` for closed questions:** each text, image or recording gets an answer from fixed options and a probability to sort by.
- **Write each question as a field:** `field_lgl()` for yes/no, `field_fct()` for a choice, with `.ordered = TRUE` for a score; add level descriptions.
- **Pass many items at once:** a character vector or a list runs in parallel and returns one tibble with `state` and `state_id`.
- **Read the low-probability rows first,** and compare a hand-labelled sample with the model's answers.

For a full workflow with codebooks, a second decision model and a human-labelled sample, see [Classifying Texts with tidyllm](https://edubruell.github.io/tidyllm/articles/tidyllm_classifiers.html).
